passages.t: ‘Endow the king with Your justice, O God’: a king for the poor
passages.happening:
The heading is short: “Of Solomon” (verse 1). The psalm is a prayer for the king. “Endow the king with Your justice, O God, and the son of the king with Your righteousness” (verse 1).

The first thing asked of him is fairness to the weak. “May he judge Your people with righteousness and Your afflicted with justice” (verse 2). “May he vindicate the afflicted among the people; may he save the children of the needy and crush the oppressor” (verse 4).

Then the prayer grows. It asks that his reign last “as long as the sun shines, as long as the moon remains” (verse 5). It asks that he be good for the land, “like rain that falls on freshly cut grass, like spring showers that water the earth” (verse 6). Under him the righteous will flourish and there will be peace “until the moon is no more” (verse 7).
passages.hearers:
Psalm 72 is one of only two psalms headed ‘of Solomon’. The other is 127. The small Hebrew word can mean ‘by’, ‘for’ or ‘about’ Solomon (the book page explains this). Some read it as Solomon's own prayer at the start of his reign. He had asked God for “an understanding heart to judge Your people” (1 Kings 3:9). Others read it as David's prayer for his son, which fits the note in verse 20. Many scholars think it was sung when a new king of David's line was crowned. The book page counts it among the royal psalms.

Kings in the ancient world often claimed to protect the weak. The Babylonian king Hammurabi wrote in his famous laws that he set them up so the strong would not oppress the weak, and to give justice to the orphan and the widow. Israel shared that ideal, but with a difference. The king's justice is not his own. It is God's justice, given to him (verse 1), and the poor are ‘Your afflicted’, God's people (verse 2).

People also believed a just reign made the land fruitful. Hence the rain on mown grass in verse 6.
passages.later:
Isaiah described a coming king of David's line in the same terms: “with righteousness He will judge the poor, and with equity He will decide for the lowly of the earth” (Isaiah 11:4). “Of the increase of His government and peace there will be no end” (Isaiah 9:7).

When Jesus began his work, he read from Isaiah: “He has anointed Me to preach good news to the poor” (Luke 4:18).
passages.asks:
The first test of a ruler in this psalm is not strength or wealth. It is how he treats the poor and those with no helper.

That test applies to anyone with power: a parent, a boss, a teacher, a leader in a church. Do the weakest people near you find you fair? Proverbs says the same: “Open your mouth for those with no voice” (Proverbs 31:8).

passages.t: ‘From sea to sea’, and ‘their blood is precious in his sight’
passages.happening:
Now the prayer reaches to the ends of the earth. “May he rule from sea to sea, and from the Euphrates to the ends of the earth” (verse 8). Kings from far away bring gifts: “may the kings of Sheba and Seba offer gifts” (verse 10). “May all kings bow down to him and all nations serve him” (verse 11).

Then the reason, and it is the heart of the psalm. “For he will deliver the needy who cry out and the afflicted who have no helper. He will take pity on the poor and needy and save the lives of the oppressed. He will redeem them from oppression and violence, for their blood is precious in his sight” (verses 12 to 14).

The psalm ends with blessing. Grain will wave on the hilltops (verse 16). “May his name endure forever” (verse 17). And in an echo of God's promise to Abraham: “In him may all nations be blessed” (verse 17).
passages.hearers:
The map in verses 8 to 10 is the whole known world as Israel saw it. The Euphrates was the great river to the north-east. Tarshish was a far port in the west. Sheba was in southern Arabia, famous for gold and spices. Its queen came to visit Solomon: “Now when the queen of Sheba heard about the fame of Solomon” (1 Kings 10:1).

Notice the word ‘for’ in verse 12. The king is honoured by the nations because he cares for the poor. His greatness rests on his mercy.

‘Their blood is precious’ means their lives matter to him. No poor person's death is cheap in his eyes.

‘In him may all nations be blessed’ takes up God's first promise to Abraham: “all the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).
passages.later:
Jesus said that “One greater than Solomon is here” (Matthew 12:42). Wise men from the east brought him “gifts of gold and frankincense and myrrh” (Matthew 2:11). Many Christians hear verses 10 and 15 in that story.

Jesus also said that what is done for the least of his brothers is done for him (Matthew 25:40). The king of Psalm 72 counts the blood of the poor as precious. So did Jesus.
passages.hard:
Who is this king? Here it is honest to say that no king of Israel ever lived up to this psalm. Solomon's reign was rich and peaceful, but he also laid heavy labour on his people (1 Kings 12:4), and his kingdom split after his death. The psalm's hope was bigger than any king who held the throne.

Jews and Christians both read it as pointing beyond those kings. An old Aramaic translation used by Jews, the Targum, adds the word ‘Messiah’ to verse 1, reading ‘the king’ as the King Messiah. Many Jewish readers look for that king still to come, who will bring justice and peace to the world. Christians read the psalm as fulfilled in Jesus, the Son of David, who reigns now and whose kingdom will one day fill the earth. The book page's part on the royal psalms sets out both readings with respect.

No modern ruler, party or nation takes the place of this king. Every ruler is measured by him.
passages.asks:
If Jesus is the king of Psalm 72, then his people should look like his kingdom. The poor and the needy should find in Christians the care this king promises.

Ask yourself: whose blood is ‘precious in my sight’? Is there anyone you have treated as if their life were cheap?

passages.t: ‘Amen and amen’: the end of Book Two
passages.happening:
After verse 17, the psalm gives way to a blessing of God. “Blessed be the LORD God, the God of Israel, who alone does marvelous deeds. And blessed be His glorious name forever; may all the earth be filled with His glory. Amen and amen” (verses 18 and 19).

Then a short note. “Thus conclude the prayers of David son of Jesse” (verse 20).
passages.hearers:
These lines close Book Two of the Psalms. The book page explains how each of the first four books ends with a short blessing of God, called a doxology. Book One ended with “Amen and Amen” (Psalm 41:13). Book Two ends here in the same way.

The note in verse 20 is a puzzle. It says David's prayers are finished, yet more than a dozen later psalms are headed ‘of David’ (86, 101, 103, 108 to 110, 122, 124, 131, 133 and 138 to 145). Many think the note once closed an earlier collection of David's psalms, before the whole book was put together, and it was left in place. Others think it simply marks the end of a section.

The blessing turns the hope of verses 1 to 17 back to God. The king's glory filling the earth (verse 17) becomes God's glory filling the earth (verse 19).
passages.later: Habakkuk shares the same hope: “For the earth will be filled with the knowledge of the glory of the LORD as the waters cover the sea” (Habakkuk 2:14). In Revelation loud voices in heaven say, “The kingdom of the world has become the kingdom of our Lord and of His Christ, and He will reign forever and ever” (Revelation 11:15).
passages.asks:
Book Two began with a thirsty man far from God's house (Psalm 42). It ends with the whole earth filled with God's glory. Thirty-one psalms lie in between: tears, guilt, betrayal, fear, old age, and praise.

That is the shape of a life with God too. The end is not yet. But you can say ‘Amen and amen’ to where it is going.
